question: Deflecting the elevator trailing edge upward primarily achieves a pitch-up by:

options.text: Directly increasing the wing's angle of attack through mechanical linkage
Reducing, or reversing, the tailplane's downward lift, producing a nose-up pitching moment that increases the wing's angle of attack
Increasing engine thrust to raise the nose
Increasing the wing's camber to generate more lift

explanation: Raising the elevator changes the tailplane's effective camber and reduces or reverses the download it normally produces to balance the aircraft. This shifts the balance of pitching moments, rotating the aircraft nose-up about its center of gravity and increasing the wing's angle of attack — the elevator acts on the tail, not directly on the wing.

question: "Adverse yaw" during a rolling manoeuvre is caused by:

options.text: The rudder being deflected in the wrong direction by the pilot
The down-going aileron producing more induced drag than the up-going aileron, yawing the nose toward the raised wing
Engine thrust asymmetry during the turn entry
The fin stalling at high angles of sideslip

explanation: To roll, one aileron deflects down, increasing lift and induced drag on that wing, while the other deflects up, decreasing both. The extra induced drag on the wing with the down-going aileron yaws the nose toward the wing that is rising — opposite to the direction of the turn — which is why it is corrected with coordinated rudder or designs such as differential or frise ailerons.

question: Deflecting the control wheel or stick to produce a roll works by:

options.text: Deflecting one aileron up and the other down, differentially changing lift and induced drag at each wingtip
Deflecting both ailerons up together
Deflecting both ailerons down together
Only moving the rudder

explanation: Ailerons always move differentially — one up, one down — so that lift increases on one wing and decreases on the other, producing the rolling moment. Moving both together in the same sense would instead change total lift symmetrically, with no roll.

question: The rudder's primary aerodynamic effect is to:

options.text: Directly roll the aircraft
Change the sideforce generated by the fin/rudder combination, yawing the aircraft about its normal axis
Change the aircraft's angle of attack directly
Control airspeed

explanation: Deflecting the rudder changes the camber and effective angle of attack of the fin/rudder assembly to the airflow, generating a sideforce that yaws the aircraft's nose about its normal (vertical) axis — the primary yaw control, though any resulting sideslip can secondarily induce some roll through dihedral effect.

question: A Frise aileron reduces adverse yaw by:

options.text: Increasing the down-going aileron's drag to match the up-going one

Shaping the aileron so that, when raised, its leading edge projects below the wing's lower surface into the airflow, deliberately adding drag on the up-going (rising wing) side to balance the down-going side's extra induced drag
Eliminating aileron drag entirely on both sides
Only operating during a stall

explanation: The Frise aileron's offset hinge means that when it deflects upward, its nose pokes down into the airflow beneath the wing, creating extra parasite drag on that (rising) wing. This helps balance the extra induced drag the opposite, down-going aileron produces, reducing the net adverse yawing moment.

question: A "differential" aileron linkage reduces adverse yaw by:

options.text: Deflecting the up-going aileron through a greater angle than the down-going one, which more closely balances the drag produced on each wing
Deflecting both ailerons by exactly the same angle in both directions
Locking the down-going aileron at neutral
Increasing both ailerons' travel equally

explanation: A differential linkage gives more mechanical travel to the up-going aileron than the down-going one. Because a large upward deflection produces relatively more drag (from the exposed lower surface) than an equally large downward one produces lift-induced drag, this asymmetric linkage helps equalise drag between the two wings.

question: An aerodynamic "horn balance" on a control surface, with part of its area ahead of the hinge line, works by:

options.text: Using airflow striking the forward horn to help move the surface, reducing the pilot's control force
Adding weight ahead of the hinge to prevent flutter
Increasing the surface's total area to increase its overall effect
Having no effect on control forces

explanation: The small area of the control surface ahead of its hinge line experiences airflow that helps drive the surface further in the direction it is being deflected, aerodynamically assisting the pilot's input and reducing the control force required — distinct from a mass balance, which is about weight, not airflow.

question: Adding a mass balance weight ahead of a control surface's hinge line is primarily intended to:

options.text: Reduce the pilot's control force required
Move the surface's center of gravity toward, or ahead of, the hinge line, preventing flutter — a potentially destructive aeroelastic oscillation
Increase the surface's aerodynamic balance area
Increase the control surface's travel

explanation: If a control surface's center of gravity sits well aft of its hinge line, structural bending of the wing or tail can excite a self-sustaining, rapidly growing oscillation called flutter. A mass balance weight forward of the hinge shifts the surface's own center of gravity to prevent this coupling.

question: "Aileron reversal" at very high airspeed can occur because:

options.text: The ailerons become disconnected mechanically
Aerodynamic loads from a deflected aileron twist a flexible wing enough that the resulting change in the wing's angle of attack produces a rolling moment opposite to the one intended
The ailerons always become more effective as speed increases, without limit
It only happens at low speed near the stall

explanation: At high dynamic pressure, the aerodynamic twisting moment from a deflected aileron can exceed the wing structure's torsional stiffness, twisting the wingtip enough to change its angle of attack in the opposite sense to what the aileron intended — overpowering, and eventually reversing, the intended roll response.

question: On some aircraft, spoilers supplement or replace ailerons for roll control by:

options.text: Extending on the down-going wing side to add lift there
Extending on the wing that is meant to drop, disrupting airflow to reduce lift (and add drag) on that side
Extending symmetrically on both wings for roll
Operating only as speed brakes, never for roll

explanation: A roll spoiler extends on the wing that is meant to go down, spoiling lift on that side (and adding drag, which also helps counter adverse yaw) — a mechanism entirely different from an aileron's differential lift, and one that can remain effective even where high-speed aileron reversal would otherwise be a concern.

question: A "stabilator" (all-moving tailplane) differs from a conventional elevator and fixed-stabilizer arrangement in that:

options.text: The entire horizontal tail surface pivots to change its angle, rather than only a hinged elevator portion moving
It has no aerodynamic effect on pitch
It is only found on gliders
It is fixed and never moves

explanation: A stabilator pivots the whole horizontal tail surface as a single unit, rather than deflecting only a hinged elevator behind a fixed stabilizer. This can provide more pitch control power, particularly useful at high speed or for aircraft needing a wide trim range, though it typically needs an anti-servo tab to give the pilot adequate feel.

question: On an aircraft with fully powered (hydraulically actuated) flight controls, an "artificial feel" system is fitted mainly because:

options.text: The actual aerodynamic forces on the control surfaces are otherwise too light for the pilot to sense

Hydraulic actuators remove virtually all natural aerodynamic feedback to the controls, so an artificial system reintroduces a feel proportional to speed and load, without which a pilot could unknowingly over-stress the aircraft
It increases the control surface's aerodynamic balance
It eliminates the need for a mass balance

explanation: A hydraulic actuator moves the control surface regardless of the aerodynamic load on it, so the pilot feels none of the natural resistance that a manually linked control would provide. An artificial feel system reintroduces a synthetic force, usually proportional to airspeed, so the pilot retains a meaningful sense of how hard the aircraft is being flown.

question: The "hinge moment" of a control surface refers to:

options.text: The aerodynamic moment about the hinge line that a pilot (or actuator) must overcome to deflect or hold the surface at a given position
The total lift the whole wing produces
The weight of the control surface alone
A measure of the aircraft's overall stability

explanation: Hinge moment is the aerodynamic moment generated about a control surface's own hinge line by the airflow acting on it, and it is what the pilot's muscular effort (or a powered actuator) must overcome to move or hold the surface at any given deflection — the physical basis of what a pilot actually feels as "control force".

question: If a control surface is left completely free (unheld and unlinked), its natural "floating tendency" is generally to:

options.text: Trail in a position where its own center of pressure aligns with the hinge line, rather than staying at neutral
Always remain locked exactly at neutral
Immediately move to its maximum deflection in one direction
Have no aerodynamic tendency to move at all

explanation: With no pilot input or mechanical restraint, a control surface tends to float to whatever angle relative to the local airflow puts its own center of pressure at the hinge line, since that is the position with zero net hinge moment — rarely exactly the neutral, streamlined position, which is why a free-floating surface (such as an unlinked servo-tab-driven elevator) is a deliberate design feature rather than an accident.

question: A control surface is said to be "aerodynamically overbalanced" when:

options.text: Its balancing area is so large or effective that, once deflected, the surface tends to move further in that same direction on its own, rather than requiring continued force
It has no aerodynamic balance area at all
It requires unusually high pilot force to move
It is balanced by a mass weight rather than an aerodynamic area

explanation: A normally balanced control needs some pilot force to hold any deflection away from neutral; an overbalanced one has so much aerodynamic assistance that, past a certain deflection, the airflow itself tends to drive the surface further in the same direction — an unstable, dangerous control-force characteristic that designers deliberately avoid.

question: A "geared" tab, distinct from a servo tab the pilot moves directly, is one that:

options.text: Is mechanically linked to move automatically, by a fixed ratio, opposite to the main surface as it deflects, purely to assist and balance the main surface's own movement
Is the pilot's sole means of moving the main control surface, which is otherwise unconnected to the cockpit controls
Only moves when the autopilot is engaged
Has no mechanical connection to the main control surface whatsoever

explanation: A geared tab is linked through gearing to deflect automatically, by a set ratio, opposite to the main surface whenever that surface moves — an aerodynamic balance aid built into the control run itself, rather than a separate control the pilot operates directly the way a servo tab is used.

question: An "internal" (or shielded) aerodynamic balance achieves the same purpose as a horn balance, but:

options.text: By enclosing a balance area within the wing or tail structure, sealed from the external slipstream, using the pressure difference across it to assist movement without an external protrusion
By adding a visible external horn projecting ahead of the hinge line
By adding weight ahead of the hinge line
By eliminating the need for any hinge at all

explanation: Rather than an external horn exposed to the airflow, an internal balance encloses part of the control surface's forward area within the fixed structure, where a pressure difference generated as the surface deflects still produces an assisting moment — achieving aerodynamic balance without the drag or exposure of an external horn.

question: The narrow gap between a fixed surface (such as a wing or tailplane) and its hinged control surface is often sealed, mainly because an open gap:

options.text: Lets air leak through from the high-pressure to the low-pressure side, reducing the control surface's effectiveness and sometimes producing buffet or noise
Always increases control effectiveness if left open
Has no aerodynamic significance whatsoever
Is required to be open for the control to move at all

explanation: An unsealed gap allows air to leak from the higher-pressure side of a deflected control surface to the lower-pressure side, undermining the pressure difference the surface is meant to create and reducing its effectiveness — which is why gaps are commonly closed with a flexible seal while still allowing free movement.

question: A "reversible" flight control system, as commonly found on light aircraft, is one in which:

options.text: Aerodynamic loads on the control surface are transmitted back through the cables or pushrods to the pilot's controls, giving natural feedback
The control surface can be moved in either direction but never returns to neutral
A hydraulic actuator isolates the pilot from all aerodynamic loads
The aircraft has no control surfaces at all

explanation: In a reversible system, the mechanical linkage between the control surface and the cockpit controls carries load in both directions, so aerodynamic forces on the surface are felt directly by the pilot — unlike an "irreversible" system (typically a powered, often hydraulic, actuator) that isolates the pilot from those loads and requires an artificial feel system instead.

question: Under a fly-by-wire aircraft's "normal law", flight control protections such as bank angle, load factor and angle-of-attack limiting typically:

options.text: Prevent the pilot's control inputs from commanding the aircraft beyond a protected envelope, even with full control deflection
Have no effect on what the pilot's inputs can command
Only apply while the aircraft is on the ground
Disable the flight controls entirely

explanation: Normal law is the fly-by-wire control mode with the fullest set of protections active, translating pilot stick or column input into a flight computer command that is kept within limits such as maximum bank angle, load factor and angle of attack — so that even full, abrupt control input cannot command the aircraft outside its protected envelope under normal conditions.

question: If certain sensors or computers fail on a fly-by-wire aircraft, it may revert to an "alternate" or "direct" control law, in which:

options.text: Some or all of the automatic envelope protections are reduced or removed, giving the pilot more direct authority but also more responsibility for staying within limits
All flight controls are disabled entirely
Protections become stronger than in normal law
The aircraft can no longer be flown manually at all

explanation: Alternate and direct law are reversionary modes used when the aircraft can no longer safely provide the full protections of normal law — control response becomes more directly tied to the pilot's input, with fewer or no automatic limits, meaning the pilot must exercise the judgement those protections would otherwise have provided.

question: Ice accumulation on a control surface or its leading edge can affect flight controls by:

options.text: Changing hinge moments, reducing aerodynamic effectiveness, and in severe cases risking a jam or an imbalance that could contribute to flutter
Always making the control surface lighter and easier to move
Having no effect on control surfaces, only on the wing
Only affecting the trim tabs, never the primary control surface itself

explanation: Ice changes the shape and weight distribution of a control surface, which can alter hinge moments and reduce aerodynamic effectiveness, restrict free movement, or in severe cases disturb the careful mass balance built into the surface — a genuine, multi-faceted hazard beyond simply adding weight.

question: On a tailless delta or flying-wing aircraft, "elevons" are trailing-edge surfaces that:

options.text: Combine the functions of elevator and aileron — moving together for pitch control and differentially for roll control
Provide yaw control only
Are used exclusively as speed brakes
Exist only on aircraft with a conventional separate tailplane

explanation: With no separate tailplane to carry a dedicated elevator, a tailless design combines pitch and roll control into the same trailing-edge surfaces: deflecting both together produces a pitching moment, while deflecting them differentially produces a rolling moment, exactly as an elevator and ailerons would separately on a conventional aircraft.

question: On a canard configuration, with a small lifting surface ahead of the main wing rather than a conventional aft tailplane, pitch control and trim are typically provided by generating:

options.text: Lift on the canard surface itself, rather than the download a conventional aft tailplane typically provides
Download on the canard, identical in principle to a conventional tail
No aerodynamic force from the canard at all — it is purely decorative
Thrust vectoring alone, with no aerodynamic surface involved

explanation: Because it sits ahead of the center of gravity, a canard surface generally needs to produce upward lift, not the download a conventional aft tailplane typically provides, to create the pitching moment needed to trim and control the aircraft — one reason some canard designs can, in principle, add total lift rather than subtracting from it the way a conventional tail's download does.

question: A rudder travel limiter, which reduces the maximum available rudder deflection as airspeed increases, exists mainly to:

options.text: Prevent a full rudder deflection at high airspeed from generating loads on the fin and rear fuselage beyond their structural design limits
Increase rudder authority at high speed
Prevent the rudder from moving at all below a certain speed
Improve fuel efficiency

explanation: The sideforce a fully deflected rudder can generate rises with dynamic pressure, and at high airspeed a full, abrupt rudder deflection (or a rapid full reversal) could load the fin and rear fuselage structure beyond its design limits. A travel limiter progressively reduces the maximum available deflection as speed increases to keep those loads within safe bounds.

question: An aircraft's susceptibility to control surface flutter is closely tied to airspeed because:

options.text: The aerodynamic energy available to drive a self-sustaining oscillation increases with dynamic pressure, so flutter tends to appear only above a certain critical speed
Flutter is equally likely at any airspeed, including when the aircraft is stationary
Flutter only occurs at very low airspeed
Airspeed has no bearing on flutter risk at all

explanation: Flutter is a self-sustaining aeroelastic oscillation fed by aerodynamic energy, and the amount of energy available from the airflow rises with dynamic pressure. Below a critical flutter speed for a given structure and mass balance, any disturbance damps out; above it, the same disturbance can grow instead — which is why flutter is treated as a speed-dependent structural limit.

question: As airspeed increases toward an aircraft's aileron reversal speed, aileron effectiveness (roll rate per unit of deflection):

options.text: Typically declines gradually well before the reversal speed itself is reached, rather than staying constant right up to that point
Remains perfectly constant right up to the exact reversal speed
Increases steadily all the way to the reversal speed
Has no relationship to wing flexibility at all

explanation: Wing twist under aileron load grows progressively with dynamic pressure, so the aerodynamic twisting effect that eventually causes full reversal at a high enough speed already erodes aileron effectiveness at speeds well below that reversal point — a gradual decline rather than a sudden effect only at the reversal speed itself.

question: For a given control surface deflection, a control surface's "control power" (the moment it generates on the aircraft) increases with:

options.text: Higher dynamic pressure (broadly, higher indicated airspeed) and a larger control surface area or moment arm from the center of gravity
Altitude alone, independent of airspeed
Outside air temperature alone
Nothing — control power is fixed regardless of speed or size

explanation: The moment a deflected control surface generates depends on the aerodynamic force it produces (which rises with dynamic pressure, and hence broadly with indicated airspeed) multiplied by its distance from the aircraft's center of gravity — so a larger surface, a longer moment arm, or a higher indicated airspeed all increase control power for the same deflection angle.

question: Critical flight control surfaces on transport aircraft are often driven by more than one hydraulic actuator, mainly to:

options.text: Provide redundancy, so the surface can still be moved if one hydraulic system or actuator fails
Increase the surface's maximum deflection angle
Reduce the aircraft's overall weight
Eliminate the need for any mass balance

explanation: Because a powered (irreversible) control system gives the pilot no mechanical fallback if its actuator fails, critical surfaces are typically driven by two or more independent actuators fed from separate hydraulic systems, so the loss of any single system or actuator still leaves the surface controllable.

question: At certain angles of sideslip, an aircraft's rudder can lose some effectiveness because:

options.text: The horizontal stabilizer or fuselage can blanket (shield) part of the fin and rudder from the oncoming airflow
The rudder always becomes more effective as sideslip angle increases, with no limit
Blanketing only affects the elevator, never the rudder
It has nothing to do with the tailplane's position

explanation: Depending on the tail's geometry, a large sideslip angle can place the horizontal stabilizer (or part of the fuselage) in a position that shields part of the fin and rudder from clean airflow, reducing the rudder's effectiveness right when a large sideslip may most need correcting — an important consideration in tail design and in spin recovery on some configurations.

question: On a propeller aircraft, the rudder and elevator often remain reasonably effective even at very low forward airspeed with high power applied, mainly because:

options.text: The propeller's slipstream passes directly over the tail surfaces, providing dynamic pressure well beyond what the aircraft's own forward speed alone would give them
Control surfaces are always equally effective regardless of any local airflow
Low forward speed always increases control effectiveness
The engine directly drives the control surfaces mechanically

explanation: Because the propeller accelerates a column of air rearward over the fuselage and tail, the tail surfaces sitting in that slipstream see a dynamic pressure much higher than the aircraft's own forward airspeed alone would produce — which is why rudder and elevator authority at high power and low airspeed (as during a slow taxi or a tailwheel liftoff) is often better than the aircraft's raw forward speed would suggest.

question: Once a control surface has been correctly trimmed for a given flight condition, the pilot needs to apply:

options.text: Essentially no sustained holding force, even though the main control surface itself may still be significantly deflected
The same holding force as before trimming, with no change at all
More force than before trimming
Force only in the opposite direction to the original out-of-trim force

explanation: The trim tab's own aerodynamic force holds the main control surface at whatever deflection balances the aircraft, so once correctly trimmed the pilot's hands can be removed from the controls with no sustained holding force needed — the trim tab, not continuous pilot effort, is doing the work.

question: At the same indicated (or calibrated) airspeed, an aircraft's control surface effectiveness at high altitude, compared with low altitude, is:

options.text: Essentially unchanged, since indicated airspeed already reflects the dynamic pressure the controls actually respond to
Always much lower at high altitude
Always much higher at high altitude
Undefined above 10,000 feet

explanation: Because indicated (or calibrated) airspeed is derived from dynamic pressure, and control surface hinge moments and effectiveness depend on that same dynamic pressure, flying at the same indicated airspeed gives essentially the same control feel and effectiveness at high altitude as at low altitude, even though the true airspeed involved is quite different.

question: A stabilator (all-moving tailplane) typically needs an anti-servo tab mainly because, without one, it would tend to be:

options.text: Dangerously sensitive and lightly damped, given its large area and comparatively small natural aerodynamic resistance to movement
Impossible to move by the pilot at all
Unaffected by any change in speed
Already perfectly damped with no assistance needed

explanation: A stabilator's whole surface pivots as one large, comparatively low-drag unit, which can leave it feeling unnaturally light and overly sensitive to small control inputs. An anti-servo tab, deflecting with the stabilator to increase the force needed to move it, restores a more natural, better-damped control feel and reduces the risk of over-controlling in pitch.

question: Some aircraft with powered flight controls are designed with a "manual reversion" capability, meaning that if hydraulic power is lost:

options.text: The pilot can still move the control surfaces directly through cables or pushrods, though typically with much higher control forces than normal
The aircraft becomes completely uncontrollable
The autopilot automatically takes over with no pilot input
Only the rudder remains controllable

explanation: A manual reversion system retains a direct mechanical link, alongside the normal powered actuation, so that a total loss of hydraulic power still leaves the pilot able to fly the aircraft — at the cost of much higher control forces than the powered system would have required, since the pilot is now overcoming the full aerodynamic hinge moment unaided.

question: If a primary flight control surface jams in flight, a possible fallback for maintaining some control of the aircraft is:

options.text: Using pitch or roll trim, and differential engine thrust where available, to influence the aircraft's attitude indirectly
There is never any alternative once a primary control has jammed
Immediately shutting down all engines
Relying solely on the landing gear for control

explanation: With a jammed primary control, pitch or roll trim surfaces (which are still independently actuated) and, on a multi-engine aircraft, differential thrust between engines can both provide a degree of indirect attitude control — documented emergency techniques that have allowed otherwise crippled aircraft to be flown to a landing.

question: On some large control surfaces, mass balance weight is distributed along the span rather than concentrated at a single point, mainly to:

options.text: Guard against both bending-related and torsional flutter modes, not just the simplest single-mode case a single concentrated weight would address
Reduce the total weight added to the aircraft
Make the control surface easier for the pilot to move
Eliminate the need for any aerodynamic balance

explanation: A long control surface can flutter in more than one mode — coupling with wing bending in one case, with torsion in another — and a single concentrated mass balance weight may only address the simplest of these. Distributing the balance mass along the span helps guard against multiple flutter modes rather than just one.

subtopic: Control Surface Sealing at High Speed
question: Maintaining a well-fitted, sealed gap around a control surface matters more, not less, as design speed increases, mainly because:

options.text: The pressure difference driving leakage through an unsealed gap grows with dynamic pressure, so the effectiveness penalty from a poor seal becomes larger at higher speed
Gap sealing is only relevant at very low airspeed
A larger gap always improves control effectiveness at high speed
Sealing has no relationship to speed at all

explanation: Because the pressure difference across a deflected control surface rises with dynamic pressure, any leakage path through a poorly sealed gap becomes a proportionally larger loss of effectiveness at higher speed — which is why gap seals and their condition are specifically checked on faster aircraft.
